ESC HF 2021: an ICD should be considered in non-ischaemic HF with "an LVEF ≤35% despite ≥3 months of OMT" (IIa A), if expected survival is >1 y with good function; ischaemic: wait ≥40 d post-MI. Many patients recover LVEF on GDMT. A wearable defibrillator can bridge selected high-risk patients; EP study and amiodarone have no role here.

references.title: ESC HF 2021, ICD recommendations (p. 27)
references.supports: ICD after ≥3 mo OMT if LVEF ≤35%
references.quote: an LVEF ≤35% despite ≥3 months of OMT

issues: Accurate: NICM primary-prevention ICD needs LVEF ≤35%, NYHA II–III after ≥3 mo GDMT, survival >1 y (ACC summary; JAMA synopsis PDF).
Option D wording 'Implant ICD before discharge from clinic' is awkward (outpatient, nothing to discharge from).
'Holter: no sustained VT' adds length without changing the decision.
Second reference is a JAMA Clinical Guidelines Synopsis hosted on a hospital site; acceptable but better cite the original.

questions.explanation_previous: A primary-prevention ICD is considered only when LVEF stays ≤35% with NYHA II–III symptoms after ≥3 months of optimized GDMT (and ≥40 d post-MI / ≥90 d post-revascularization if ischemic), with expected survival >1 y. Many patients improve on GDMT and no longer need a device.

guideline_review.note: ICD considered only after ≥3 months OMT with persistent LVEF ≤35% supports B. ESC grades non-ischaemic ICD IIa (after DANISH) rather than I.

questions.stem: 66F w/ COPD discharged today after 5d admission for an exacerbation. Now stable on triple inhaler therapy. Never attended rehab.
questions.lead: Most appropriate timing to start pulmonary rehabilitation?

options.label: B
options.explanation: Delay loses benefit; risk of readmission is highest early.

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.explanation: Correct: ERS/ATS; fewer readmissions and better quality of life.

options.label: E

questions.explanation: Pulmonary rehab soon after a COPD admission reduces readmissions and improves quality of life, yet few patients are referred. ERS/ATS 2017: "we suggest the initiation of pulmonary rehabilitation within 3 weeks after hospital discharge", and suggest not starting it during the hospitalisation. Refer at discharge rather than waiting months or for repeat spirometry; early rehab is also associated with lower 1-year mortality.

references.title: ERS/ATS COPD exacerbations 2017, Q6 (PDF p. 13)
references.quote: we suggest the initiation of pulmonary rehabilitation within 3 weeks after hospital discharge

issues: Accurate: ERS/ATS 2017 suggests not starting PR during admission and starting within 3 wk of discharge.
Lead asks for timing but options A and C are about eligibility, not timing: heterogeneous options.
Reference ERJ 51/1/1701312 failed to load; verified via the ATS-hosted PDF of the same guideline.
JAMA 2020 mortality association is for initiation within 90 d, not specifically 3–4 wk; explanation slightly overstates.

questions.explanation_previous: ERS/ATS suggest starting pulmonary rehabilitation within 3 weeks of discharge after a COPD exacerbation (fewer readmissions, better quality of life) and suggest against starting it during the admission. Starting rehab soon after discharge is associated with lower 1-y mortality, yet uptake is very low.

guideline_review.note: Within 3 weeks after discharge, and not during admission; supports D.

questions.stem: 46M w/ first proximal DVT 3 wk after knee arthroplasty. No prior VTE. Father had a DVT at 70 after hip fracture. Started on apixaban.

questions.explanation: DVT after major surgery has a low recurrence risk once the provoking factor is gone, so treat ~3 months and stop. ASH 2023: "For patients with VTE provoked by surgery who have completed primary short-term treatment, the ASH guideline panel suggests not to perform thrombophilia testing". A distant relative's provoked clot doesn't change this. Contrast: ASH now suggests testing after VTE provoked by nonsurgical major transient factors, pregnancy or estrogen, where a positive result would favour indefinite anticoagulation.

references.quote: the ASH guideline panel suggests not to perform thrombophilia testing

In contrast, ASH now suggests testing after VTE provoked by nonsurgical major transient factors (e.g., pregnancy, estrogen) to guide duration — a change from older advice.

guideline_review.note: R2 supports no testing and stopping after primary treatment (C).

questions.stem: 27F nurse sustained a deep hollow-bore needlestick 2 h ago from a patient w/ known HIV; source's current viral load and ART adherence unknown. She is HIV-negative at baseline.

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: Start PEP only if she seroconverts
options.explanation: Then it's treatment of HIV, not prophylaxis.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Regimens are 3 drugs for 28 days.

options.label: E
options.text: Await source viral load before deciding
options.explanation: Delay reduces efficacy; start now and reassess when results return.

questions.explanation: After a high-risk needlestick from an HIV-positive source, start PEP immediately, ideally within hours and no later than 72 h. USPHS 2013: PEP "should be started as soon as possible after occupational exposure to HIV", continued for 4 weeks, with 3 or more drugs (e.g., tenofovir/FTC plus an integrase inhibitor such as dolutegravir or raltegravir). Don't wait for source viral load; if the source proves suppressed, stopping is a shared decision.

references.title: USPHS Occupational HIV PEP Guidelines 2013 (p. 875)
references.quote: should be started as soon as possible after occupational exposure to HIV

issues: Keyed answer correct.
Reference 1 is a 2023 CDC draft slide deck (explicitly not policy). The final 2025 USPHS occupational PEP guideline is now published (Infect Control Hosp Epidemiol 2025).

Explanation should reflect 2025 preferred regimens (BIC/FTC/TAF, or DTG + TAF/TDF + FTC/3TC) and note that a suppressed source now triggers shared decision-making, which is why waiting for VL is wrong when it is unknown.
CMAJ 2017 reference addresses nonoccupational PEP; acceptable for 72 h/28 d only.

questions.explanation_previous: Start PEP as soon as possible, ideally within hours and no later than 72 h, for 28 days, with a 3-drug integrase-inhibitor regimen (e.g., bictegravir/FTC/TAF, or dolutegravir + tenofovir + FTC/3TC). Don't wait for source testing; if the source proves to have an undetectable viral load, stopping is a shared decision.

guideline_review.note: PEP started ASAP, continued 4 wk, ≥3 drugs for all occupational exposures; don't delay for source testing. Keyed B matches. Preferred drugs in 2013 were TDF/FTC + raltegravir; the explanation's newer INSTI options reflect current practice (not quoted).

Cr 88 µmol/L

questions.stem:
68F w/ nonischemic cardiomyopathy, NYHA III despite 6 mo of target-dose sacubitril-valsartan, bisoprolol, spironolactone and dapagliflozin. Sinus rhythm.

TTE: LVEF 28%
ECG: LBBB, QRS 162 ms

options.label: A
options.explanation: Already on optimized GDMT for months; delay isn't warranted.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Not before CRT; requires sinus HR ≥70 and has smaller benefit.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Symptomatic only; doesn't address dyssynchrony.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Misses resynchronization benefit given LBBB and QRS ≥150.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Correct: LVEF ≤35%, sinus rhythm, LBBB, QRS ≥150 ms on GDMT.

questions.explanation: CRT has its strongest indication in symptomatic HFrEF with LVEF ≤35%, sinus rhythm and LBBB with QRS ≥150 ms despite optimized GDMT (≥3 mo). ESC HF 2021 (Class I A): "CRT is recommended for symptomatic patients with HF in SR with a QRS duration ≥150 ms and LBBB". It improves symptoms, hospitalizations and survival; a CRT-D is usually chosen. Benefit is weaker with non-LBBB or QRS 130–149 ms; ivabradine and digoxin don't address dyssynchrony.

questions.stem:
58M w/ HTN, 3 episodes of symptomatic typical (counterclockwise) atrial flutter in 1 y despite metoprolol; cardioverted each time. No documented AF. On apixaban.

TTE: normal LVEF, mild LA enlargement

options.label: A
options.explanation: Correct: cures >90% of typical flutter; superior to drugs for recurrence.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Last-resort rate control, not rhythm control.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Less effective and more toxic than ablation.

options.label: D
options.explanation: AF ablation; typical flutter is a right-atrial circuit.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Class IC drugs are less effective than ablation; IC alone risks 1:1 conduction.

questions.explanation: Typical (counterclockwise) flutter is a macro-re-entry through the cavotricuspid isthmus; ablating the isthmus cures >90% and beats antiarrhythmics. ESC SVT 2019 (Class I A): "Catheter ablation is recommended for symptomatic, recurrent episodes of CTI-dependent flutter", and it should be considered even after a first episode (IIa). PVI targets AF; AV node ablation is a last resort. Anticoagulate as for AF by CHA2DS2-VASc, including after ablation, because AF often develops later.

references.title: ESC SVT 2019, macro-re-entrant atrial arrhythmia recs (p. 25)
references.quote: Catheter ablation is recommended for symptomatic, recurrent episodes of CTI-dependent flutter

issues: Answer correct: Merck states CTI ablation cures typical flutter in >95% and prevents recurrence more effectively than antiarrhythmics + AV nodal blockade; anticoagulation guidelines don't distinguish flutter from AF; AF occurs in up to 60% within 10 y.

Option 'Flecainide + metoprolol long term' explanation is inaccurate as written: the co-prescribed AV nodal blocker is what mitigates 1:1 conduction, so the explanation implies the regimen itself causes 1:1 conduction.
'continuing >=4 wk after ablation' was not verifiable in the opened sources (PMC table returned CAPTCHA); long-term OAC is decided by CHA2DS2-VASc, which is the more important teaching point.
Second reference (PMC table) could not be opened (CAPTCHA).

questions.explanation_previous: Typical flutter depends on the cavotricuspid isthmus; ablating it cures >90% and is preferred over antiarrhythmics for recurrent episodes. Anticoagulate flutter exactly as AF (same risk scores), including after ablation, since AF later develops in up to 60%.

guideline_review.note: Class I A CTI ablation for recurrent typical flutter supports A. ESC gives flutter without AF a IIa (not I) for anticoagulation; patient is already anticoagulated, CHA2DS2-VASc-based approach unchanged.

questions.topic: Graves' hyperthyroidism in the first trimester

TSH <0.01 mIU/L

questions.explanation: Overt Graves' hyperthyroidism in pregnancy needs antithyroid drug treatment; in the first trimester use PTU, because methimazole causes embryopathy during organogenesis. ATA 2016 (Rec 80, strong): "PTU should be used when ATD therapy is given during the first trimester. MMI should be used when ATD therapy is started after the first trimester." Use the lowest dose keeping free T4 at or just above the upper reference limit, and recheck TRAb later in pregnancy. Radioiodine is contraindicated; surgery only if ATDs fail.

references.quote: PTU should be used when ATD therapy is given during the first trimester.

questions.explanation_previous: For overt Graves' hyperthyroidism in the first trimester, PTU is preferred because methimazole is associated with embryopathy during organogenesis; consider switching to methimazole after the first trimester (PTU hepatotoxicity). Use the lowest dose keeping free T4 at or just above the upper reference limit. Repeat TRAb later in pregnancy.

guideline_review.note: Rec 80 supports PTU in first trimester (D). ATA 2017 pregnancy guideline is concordant; switching to MMI after the first trimester is optional (Rec 88, no recommendation).

questions.stem:

questions.explanation: Achalasia causes dysphagia to solids and liquids with regurgitation. EGD comes first to exclude pseudoachalasia (tumour at the GEJ) but can't confirm the diagnosis. ACG 2020: "The diagnosis of achalasia is confirmed with high-resolution manometry (HRM), which is the current gold standard test". HRM shows impaired LES relaxation with absent peristalsis, and its subtype (I–III) guides therapy. Timed barium esophagram is complementary.

AASLD 2021: "The recommended dose of albumin replacement, based on expert opinion, is 6-8 g for every liter of ascites removed." That's about 50–60 g of 25% albumin for 8 L. questions.stem:
48F w/ 5d of mild calf discomfort after a long flight. Fully mobile; no cancer, prior VTE or pregnancy.

Whole-leg US: short thrombus in one soleal (muscular) calf vein; popliteal and proximal veins clear

options.label: D

CHEST 2021: "without severe symptoms or risk factors for extension" it suggests "serial imaging of the deep veins for 2 weeks over anticoagulation", repeating US weekly (or with worse symptoms). Give no anticoagulation if it doesn't extend, anticoagulate if it extends (strongly if into proximal veins). Severe symptoms or risk factors (positive D-dimer, >5 cm or near-proximal clot, unprovoked, cancer, prior VTE, inpatient) favour 3 months of anticoagulation.

Guideline Central reference is a login page; CHEST PDF is fine.

62F w/ new GCA starting prednisone 50 mg daily, planned taper over ≥12 mo. No prior fracture.

questions.topic: Prior contrast reaction: next contrast CT
questions.stem: 58F needs contrast-enhanced CT abdomen for suspected abscess. 2 y ago she had generalized urticaria (no hypotension or bronchospasm) after iohexol; resolved w/ cetirizine. No other allergies.
questions.lead: Per current Canadian guidance, best strategy?

options.explanation: Unnecessary; reactions are agent-specific.

options.label: B

options.label: C

questions.explanation: Contrast reactions are to the contrast molecule, not iodine, and risk applies to the same agent class. questions.explanation: Fever ≥39 °C or rigors during transfusion is high-risk: it may be FNHTR, but bacterial contamination and acute hemolysis must be excluded. questions.explanation: Intranasal corticosteroids are the most effective treatment for moderate–severe allergic rhinitis, including congestion, and work best used daily. AAAAI/ACAAI Rhinitis 2020 (CBS 12): "We recommend that when choosing monotherapy for persistent allergic rhinitis, intranasal corticosteroids be the preferred medication." They also beat montelukast for seasonal AR. First-generation antihistamines are not recommended, and topical decongestants are for short-term use only.

references.title: AAAAI/ACAAI Rhinitis Practice Parameter 2020 (Table 3, CBS 12)
references.supports: INCS preferred monotherapy; preferred over LTRA
references.quote: We recommend that when choosing monotherapy for persistent allergic rhinitis, intranasal corticosteroids be the preferred medication

issues: Accurate in substance: INCS is most effective and preferred over montelukast, and adding an oral antihistamine to INCS adds no benefit (JTF 2017).

The keyed option contradicts its own explanation. 'Add a daily intranasal corticosteroid' (on top of cetirizine) goes against the guideline's INCS monotherapy recommendation, which the explanation cites.
Yield: lower for RC IM (primary-care topic). Acceptable as an allergy item.

They outperform montelukast, and adding an oral antihistamine to them adds little; an intranasal antihistamine can be added if needed. Allergen immunotherapy is an option for refractory cases.

guideline_review.note: CBS 12 (INCS preferred monotherapy) and GRADE 14 (INCS over LTRA for initial moderate–severe SAR) support C; GRADE 28 advises against initial oral antihistamine + INCS combination, matching the explanation.

questions.stem:
86F, day 2 after hip fracture repair. Nurse reports she was calm this morning but now picks at sheets and can't keep track of the conversation. Alert. Can't recite months backward; speech rambling.

T 37.2, SpO2 95%
Na 136, glucose 6.4 mmol/L
questions.lead: Which findings satisfy the CAM algorithm?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Lacks acute onset and inattention.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Lacks acute onset/fluctuating course.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Lacks acute onset; disorientation and memory aren't CAM features.

options.label: D
options.explanation: CAM: features 1 and 2, plus 3 or 4.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Lacks inattention, which is mandatory.

questions.explanation: The CAM diagnoses delirium with (1) acute onset or fluctuating course AND (2) inattention, plus EITHER (3) disorganized thinking OR (4) altered level of consciousness. This alert patient has 1, 2 and 3. CCSMH: "The Confusion Assessment Method (CAM) is recommended as a delirium screening instrument and diagnostic aid". Next, look for precipitants (pain, opioids, urinary retention, infection, hypoxia) and use nonpharmacologic measures.

references.title: CCSMH Delirium Guideline pocket card (screening)
references.supports: CAM recommended for screening and diagnosis
references.quote: The Confusion Assessment Method (CAM) is recommended as a delirium screening instrument and diagnostic aid

issues: Accurate: the CAM algorithm needs features 1 and 2 plus either 3 or 4.
Diagnosis given away: the lead names delirium, so this is pure criteria recall.
Cueing: the keyed option 'Acute/fluctuating course + inattention + disorganized thinking' is noticeably longer and is the only one built from all CAM terms.
No duplication with bank im-261030-88 (delirium management).
The PubMed reference (2240918) hit reCAPTCHA; the QUT CAM PDF supports everything.

questions.explanation_previous: The CAM diagnoses delirium when there is (1) acute onset or fluctuating course AND (2) inattention, plus EITHER (3) disorganized thinking OR (4) altered level of consciousness. This patient has features 1, 2 and 3, despite being alert. Next, look for precipitants (pain, opioids, retention, infection, hypoxia) and use nonpharmacologic measures.

guideline_review.note: CCSMH recommends CAM; its CAM table requires A (acute onset/fluctuation) and B (inattention) plus C (disorganized thinking) or D (altered consciousness). Keyed D matches. The CAM table itself is copyrighted, so only the recommendation is quoted.
